---
name: nonvacuity-witness-must-satisfy-the-binders
description: A non-vacuity witness that negates the conclusion but violates a binder proves nothing, and the degenerate object is exactly where that happens
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

A non-vacuity check must exhibit a witness inside the region the theorem **quantifies over**, not
merely one where the conclusion fails. My theorem took `(f, V)` with `V ≠ ⊤` and concluded "f is
non-injective on some test". I offered `restrictChart f ⊥` as the injective witness. True — and
worthless: `↥(⊥ : X.Opens)` has a subsingleton open lattice, so it admits **no** `V ≠ ⊤` and the
theorem cannot be instantiated there at all. Worse, injectivity was free for it anyway
(`yoneda.obj ↥⊥` is subsingleton-valued), so the landed lemma I cited was doing no work either.

**Why:** the degenerate object is the first thing you reach for when you need "an object where P
fails", and it is the most likely object to violate a *side* binder — precisely because being
degenerate is what makes P fail. So the two failure modes correlate, and the check passes review
because everyone reads the conclusion and nobody re-reads the binder list.

**How to apply:** write the witness as a full instantiation of the theorem's own signature,
including the side conditions, and *compose it with the theorem* — if the composition typechecks
you have a real refutation of the antecedent; if it doesn't, the witness is out of domain. Here
that was `not_pointwiseCoverage_specSecMap`, three lines, and it is what turned a decorative
check into `Spec k` + tautological section with `⊥ ≠ ⊤` genuinely available. Related:
[[statement-vacuity-vs-proof-vacuity]], [[a-control-that-cannot-fail-differently]],
[[two-refutations-are-not-inhabitation]].
